TIP 1: Internally inconsistent procurement account
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 01 May 2026

I am reporting procurement fraud at Alder County Facilities. I joined the office on 15 June 2025 as a contract administrator, but I personally attended the bid committee meeting on 04 March 2025 where the East Annex cleaning contract was redirected to Lumen Janitorial.

The contract file says Lumen's winning bid was $1,240,000. The three line items I list from the same bid are $410,000 for labor, $275,000 for supplies, and $190,000 for supervision, which I also say equals the full contract value. I know those numbers do not match the award memo, but both are in the records I copied.

I was on approved medical leave from 01 March 2025 through 20 March 2025 and did not have building access during that period. I still remember watching Facilities Director Caro Bell sign the 04 March evaluation sheet in person. The witness Raj Mehta was a junior analyst on the first page of my notes and the chief compliance officer on the last page.

There are other details I cannot reconcile. I wrote in my notes that the losing bidder, Voss Cleaning, submitted a $780,000 proposal, but later I wrote that Voss was disqualified because it never submitted a price proposal. I also wrote that the award was approved by the county board on 10 March, then said the bid committee changed the scores after the board approval on 18 March. I am including all of this because these are the notes I kept, even though the sequence does not line up cleanly.

TIP 2: Internally consistent two-year procurement scheme
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 02 May 2026

I worked as procurement coordinator for Briar Port Authority from 03 January 2024 through 30 April 2026. This report concerns three maintenance contracts awarded to Seaward Mechanical during my tenure.

Contract BPA-M-2407 for pump repair closed on 12 July 2024 and was awarded on 29 July 2024 for $840,000. Contract BPA-M-2511 for dockside valve replacement closed on 06 March 2025 and was awarded on 21 March 2025 for $1,180,000. Contract BPA-M-2602 for winterization work closed on 09 January 2026 and was awarded on 24 January 2026 for $620,000.

In each file, Deputy Director Wallace Frayne added an "emergency readiness" score after bid close. The added points moved Seaward from second to first. I have the original score sheets, the revised sheets, and Frayne's emails to evaluator Mina Sol dated 26 July 2024, 19 March 2025, and 22 January 2026. The total value of the three awards is $2,640,000.

The pattern is visible in the file history. The original score sheets were saved before the evaluation meetings, while the revised sheets were saved one or two days before each award memo. In all three procurements, Seaward's price was higher than the first-ranked bidder before the emergency-readiness category was added. The procurement manual dated 01 May 2023 requires any scoring change after bid close to be approved by the general counsel, and I found no such approval in any of the three folders.

TIP 3: Vague but coherent workplace concern
CHANNEL: web form
RECEIVED: 03 May 2026

I work at a company in the operations department. For a couple of years, a senior person has been changing numbers before reports go outside the company. I am not comfortable giving names, dates, system names, customer names, or amounts because the group is small and I could be identified.

The pattern is consistent. A report is prepared by staff, then a manager asks for changes that make the results look better. The changed version is sent outside the company, while the original version stays in an internal folder. This has happened more than once and several people have seen it.

I do not have permission to share files right now. I am writing because someone outside the company should know that the official reports are not the same as the internal ones.

I understand this may be too vague to act on. I am leaving out details deliberately because I still work there and the reports are handled by a very small team. The issue is not a one-time typo or a formatting difference. It is a repeated practice where internal numbers are softened before they are sent to people outside the company.

TIP 4: Reference-rich shell company payment report
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 04 May 2026

I am a treasury analyst at Rowan Medical Devices, 455 Brackett Street, Stamford, Connecticut. On 14 November 2025, Rowan wired $742,118.43 from First Atlantic Bank account ending 9081 to Veridian Advisory Limited, a Cyprus entity listed at 12 Iasonos Street, Limassol.

The payment was booked against invoice VAD-2025-447 for "market access support" on purchase order PO-77148. The approval chain in Oracle shows CFO Patrice Noll approved it at 8:41 AM and General Counsel Evan Thorne approved it at 8:46 AM. There is no executed services agreement in the legal drive folder `LEGAL/ROWAN/VENDORS/VERIDIAN`.

I have the SWIFT confirmation MT103 reference FABKUS33-251114-00682, the Oracle approval screenshot, the 12 November 2025 board minutes at page 7, and an email from Controller Mae Shin asking why a Cyprus vendor was being paid from the regulatory affairs cost center.

The payment description also conflicts with the project code used in Oracle. Invoice VAD-2025-447 was charged to cost center RA-204, which is used for FDA submissions, but the invoice refers to "market access support in Central Europe." The vendor master file was created on 10 November 2025 by procurement analyst Jonah Bell and approved the same day by Thorne. The wire was released four days later, before tax documentation was uploaded.

TIP 5: Procedural report of serious conduct
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 05 May 2026

Subject: Review request for Meridian Hospice billing records

I am a coding auditor at Meridian Hospice. I reviewed claims submitted between 01 October 2025 and 31 December 2025 for the Cleveland service area. The review identified 46 claims where general inpatient hospice care was billed although the nursing notes documented routine home care.

The claims were approved by Regional Billing Manager Daria Kline. The affected claim IDs are listed in spreadsheet `CLE-GIP-Q4-review.xlsx`; the total reimbursement difference is $128,440. I raised the issue to Compliance Officer Harlan Cho on 22 January 2026 and received no substantive response.

Available records include the claim list, nursing notes, billing approvals, and my email to compliance. I am requesting external review because the claims remain submitted.

This report is limited to the Cleveland service area because that is the queue I audited. I have not reviewed other regions and do not know whether the pattern exists elsewhere. The relevant records can be checked by comparing the level-of-care field in the submitted claim to the nursing note for the same service date.

TIP 6: Furious but specific billing complaint
CHANNEL: intake form
RECEIVED: 06 May 2026

I am sick over what Meridian Hospice did. It is disgusting to watch managers turn patients into billing codes and then act like anyone who objects is the problem. I have been crying after shifts because this is so wrong.

The facts are still clear. In the Cleveland service area, Regional Billing Manager Daria Kline approved general inpatient hospice billing for routine home care notes during Q4 2025. I saw claim IDs MH-CLE-8810 through MH-CLE-8822 in the audit queue on 18 December 2025. The difference on those thirteen claims alone was $31,780.

I know this sounds angry because I am angry. These were real patient files and real public money. I have screenshots of the billing queue, the nursing notes, and Kline's approval comments saying "use GIP where defensible."

I reported this internally and felt like I was treated as hysterical for caring. Compliance Officer Harlan Cho said on 22 January 2026 that the coding was "within tolerance," which made me feel like I was losing my mind. I am not trying to make a political point. I want someone to look at the claims and tell the staff that this is not just normal billing pressure.

TIP 7: Non-ideological report of inventory diversion
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 07 May 2026

I am a materials coordinator at Stonebridge Public Hospital. This report concerns missing orthopedic implants from the central supply room between 06 January 2026 and 28 February 2026.

Inventory logs show 38 Stryker tibial baseplates removed under manual override codes. The corresponding surgeries account for 24 units. Supply supervisor Nolan Crewe approved the overrides and signed the weekly reconciliation reports. The unexplained difference is 14 units, with an inventory value of $96,600.

I have the Lawson inventory export, the surgical case list, and the reconciliation reports. I am submitting this because the records should be reviewed by someone outside the supply chain department.

I have not accused any particular person of taking the implants because I did not see a removal outside the system. The reason Crewe matters is that his approval appears on the override records and the weekly reconciliations. The discrepancy may have an explanation, but the same department that approved the overrides should not be the only department reviewing it.

TIP 8: Calm ideological framing with concrete facts
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 08 May 2026

I am submitting this as part of the Civic Procurement Accountability Network, a local organization documenting how privatized public services transfer public money to politically connected vendors. The attached concern about Stonebridge Public Hospital is one example of that broader pattern.

The concrete issue is an implant inventory discrepancy. Between 06 January 2026 and 28 February 2026, 38 Stryker tibial baseplates were removed from central supply under manual override codes, while surgical records account for 24 units. Supply supervisor Nolan Crewe approved the overrides. The unexplained inventory value is $96,600.

Our organization intends to use this case in a public campaign against outsourcing and patronage in hospital procurement. I am calm about the facts, but I am not neutral about the system that produces them. I can provide the Lawson export and campaign research file on request.

We are comparing this discrepancy to two other hospital purchasing cases because we believe public institutions lose accountability when supply-chain functions are treated as technical back-office work. Stonebridge is not being singled out randomly. It fits the pattern our campaign is designed to expose: public money, private vendors, weak internal review, and managers approving exceptions without independent scrutiny.
